messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol is a 47-year-old Latina woman who has spent most of her adult life working in social ministry, visiting parish families in crisis, organizing meals, and sitting with people through illness and loss. She had once understood herself as someone steady, warm, and deeply sustained by faith. The rape happened eight months ago after an evening ministry meeting, when she stayed late to lock up and finish paperwork. In the near-empty building, the quiet of the hallway had felt ordinary at first. What remains with her now is not a continuous story but a series of fixed images: the fluorescent light over the side entrance, a hand closing over her mouth, the pattern of the floor seen sideways, her blouse twisted against her skin. When she tries to speak about it, she stalls and says she knows exactly what happened but cannot get the words out in order. Each return of those picture-like moments brings a rush of guilt so intense that she drops her eyes and says she should have left earlier, should have known, should have done something different. Remembering it this way has hardened into something broader: shame about her body, a sense that happiness has gone out of her life for good, and a painful loss of trust not only in people but in the God she had relied on for years.

Those meanings now shape how she lives with herself. Because she has come to believe that her body is spoiled and that she deserves to suffer, she refuses herself ordinary comfort. She avoids relaxing in the evenings with her husband, even on the couch in their own home, because any softening of vigilance feels wrong and unsafe, almost like letting something happen again. She has also begun to eat in a tightly controlled way, skipping meals and restricting portions with the feeling that if she can master hunger, she can at least master something. There is a punishing quality to this that she recognizes: on bad days she tells herself she should not be allowed ease. The same beliefs have altered how she reads the world around her. Silence no longer feels peaceful; it feels loaded, as if danger is gathering just outside awareness. If a colleague is late returning from a home visit or a parishioner takes too long to answer a knock at the office door, Marisol’s mind goes immediately to catastrophe. Even when she can state, rationally, that she is in a safe place, she cannot relax into that knowledge.

Her memory of the assault intensifies this vigilance. In the ministry office, if the hallway suddenly goes quiet after a burst of activity, one of those still images flashes into her mind and her body tightens before she has fully understood why. Delays are especially potent because the attack took shape in an ordinary in-between time, when she had expected to leave and instead was trapped. When something runs longer than expected, she feels the same helpless dread rising. The snapshots do not come with a full narrative she can tell herself through; they arrive as fragments, and in the gap where words should be, threat fills in. Afterward she is often even harsher with herself, as though the mere fact that she can still be thrown back into those moments proves she has been permanently changed for the worse.

Over the months, Marisol has built her days around trying not to feel overwhelmed, but those efforts have narrowed her life and kept the experience raw. At work she avoids sitting alone in a quiet room between appointments and keeps herself moving through noisy, practical tasks. At home she stays busy late into the evening folding laundry or cleaning the kitchen because being still feels dangerous. She controls her eating most rigidly on days when the images are close to the surface, and the self-punishing thoughts become louder after she remembers. Yet the constant tension leaves her scanning for danger all the time, more reactive to silence and delay, less able to settle. The less she allows herself rest, the more foreign and unreachable calm has become. And because she has not been able to put the assault into words, the memory remains trapped in those stark pictures, returning with the same guilt and bodily shame each time.

This has changed her marriage and her work. Her husband has begun to say she is physically present but never at ease, always braced. In the parish, she still shows up for others, but she times visits to avoid being alone in the building and feels ashamed that a ministry built on trust now unfolds for her in a world that seems fundamentally unsafe. What finally brought her to treatment was a recent afternoon when a client was late, the office fell silent, and Marisol felt certain something terrible was happening; afterward she went home, could not eat, and sat rigid for hours, unable to pray. She is seeking help because she is frightened that this miserable, watchful version of herself is all that is left, and because some part of her still hopes she might recover a way to live in her body, with other people, and with God that does not feel governed by danger.
